brief_context: Discovered the principle of fibre optics in the thirties.
article_title: The Supply Industry - leader in the development and use of FIBRE OPTICS
brief_extract:
Fibre optics development, said to be at
the same stage now that the radio
transmitter had reached at the turn of the
century, looks like firing an explosion
beside which the computer explosion and
the video explosion will look like mere
squibs. The principle was discovered in the
’thirties by John Logie Baird, that engineer
who was found unsatisfactory by the Clyde
Valley Electrical Power Company but who
nevertheless went on to develop TV and
even produced a forerunner to radar called
Noctovisor. Simply, the principle is that a beam of
light entering a glass tube loses none of its
strength through the sides but reaches the
other end undimmed.

article_title: FOCUS : 2000 THE NEW STRATEGY — and WHAT IT IS ALL ABOUT
brief_extract: It is not a blueprint for the future so much as a framework upon which the future of the EAW can grow at its own pace. The main features are the formation of The Electric Living Foundation (to be dedicated to the memory of the late Miss Mary George, CBE) as a special unit seeking corporate patronage from those sectors of electrical commerce and industry which do not already make contributions; the introduction of new branch objectives in the form of worthwhile long term projects from which choices can be made; a commitment to take a fresh look, together with the Federation Advisory Council, at membership and the question of how to make it more relevant and appealing to people today; an intention, similarly, to discuss the appropriateness or otherwise of the Association's title, with an eye to the future; and lastly, but by no means least in importance, a wholehearted effort to improve the fortunes and functions of the Caroline Haslett Memorial Trust. Taken in isolation, the constituent parts of this strategy are worthwhile enough in themselves as timely reforms but, when brought together, they constitute an extremely effective launch-pad for the EAW's work in tomorrow's world — and that begins in 1985.

The six decades of EAW life have borne hallmarks of their particular social and historical backgrounds, illustrating the Association's lasting ability to respond to the specific needs of successive eras. brief_extract: In June 1926, some two years after the formation of the EAW, the first issue of the Association's journal, then called The Electrical Age for Women and edited by Miss Caroline Haslett, appeared. We give below some extracts from early issues which, we think, readers will find interesting, amusing and even surprising.

Women's inventions naturally have a special interest for us, particularly one by a member of our Association.
